questions.q: State the two fundamental reasons why the first element of each group in the second period shows anomalous behavior compared to the rest of the group.
questions.a: The two fundamental reasons are: (1) exceptionally small atomic size leading to high charge‑to‑radius ratio and high electronegativity, and (2) the absence of low‑lying d‑orbitals in the valence shell (only 2s and 2p orbitals are available), which restricts the maximum covalency to four and prevents expansion of the octet. A wrong answer that only mentions "small size" without the orbital limitation reveals an incomplete understanding of why heavier congeners can exceed a covalency of four.

questions.q: Explain why boron forms only BF₄⁻ while aluminium forms AlF₆³⁻, even though both are in Group 13.
questions.a: Boron (2s²2p¹) has only four valence orbitals (2s, 2pₓ, 2pᵧ, 2p_z) and no accessible 2d orbitals, so it can accommodate at most four electron pairs (sp³ hybridization) giving a maximum covalency of 4. Aluminium (3s²3p¹) has nine valence orbitals (3s, 3p, 3d) and can use sp³d² hybridization to form six bonds, hence AlF₆³⁻ exists. If a student claims it is due to electronegativity alone, they are confusing the thermodynamic driving force with the orbital‑availability constraint.

questions.q: Predict the formula of the stable fluoride anion of silicon and germanium. Justify your prediction using the concept of maximum covalency.
questions.a: Silicon (second period? No, Si is third period) – wait, silicon is in period 3. The question should compare carbon (period 2) and silicon (period 3). Let me rephrase: Predict the stable fluoride anions of carbon and silicon. Carbon forms CF₄ (neutral) but not CF₆²⁻ because its maximum covalency is 4. Silicon can form SiF₆²⁻ (hexafluorosilicate) because it has 3d orbitals available for sp³d² hybridization. A wrong answer that says both form MF₆²⁻ ignores the orbital restriction on second period elements.

questions.q: Compare the ability of nitrogen and phosphorus to form multiple bonds with oxygen. Why does N≡N exist as a stable diatomic molecule while P₄ is the stable allotrope of phosphorus?
questions.a: Nitrogen (2p orbitals) forms strong pπ–pπ multiple bonds (N≡N) due to effective sidewise overlap of small, similarly sized 2p orbitals. Phosphorus (3p orbitals) has larger, more diffuse orbitals; pπ–pπ overlap is weaker, so phosphorus prefers single bonds in P₄ tetrahedra. A student who attributes this solely to electronegativity misses the critical role of orbital size and overlap efficiency.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "The diagonal relationship between Li and Mg arises because their atomic radii are nearly identical." Is this sufficient? What other factor must be considered?
questions.a: The statement is insufficient. While Li (152 pm) and Mg (160 pm) have similar metallic radii, the diagonal relationship also requires comparable charge densities (ionic charge/ionic radius). Li⁺ (76 pm) and Mg²⁺ (72 pm) have very similar ionic radii, but Mg²⁺ carries double the charge, giving a charge density close to that of Li⁺. This similar charge density leads to comparable polarizing power, hydration enthalpies, and covalent character in compounds. A student who only cites atomic radii overlooks the charge factor.

questions.q: Design a simple experiment using household materials to demonstrate that beryllium chloride (BeCl₂) is more covalent than magnesium chloride (MgCl₂). (Hint: consider solubility in organic solvents or hydrolysis behavior.)
questions.a: A good answer: Dissolve equal amounts of BeCl₂ and MgCl₂ in ethanol. BeCl₂ dissolves readily (covalent character) while MgCl₂ is poorly soluble (ionic). Alternatively, add water: BeCl₂ hydrolyzes violently with fumes of HCl due to high charge density of Be²⁺, whereas MgCl₂ dissolves without immediate hydrolysis. A poor answer that only tests electrical conductivity in aqueous solution fails because both conduct when dissolved in water; the key is to probe covalent character via non‑polar solvents or hydrolysis kinetics.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The anomalous properties of second period elements refer to the distinct deviations in physical and chemical behavior exhibited by the first member of each group (Li, Be, B, C, N, O, F) compared to the subsequent members of the same group in the p‑block and s‑block, arising from their exceptionally small atomic size, high charge‑to‑radius ratio, high ______, and the availability of only four valence orbitals (2s and 2p) for bonding.
Fill in the blank: Begin by showing a student a piece of lithium metal (soft, silvery) and a strip of ______ ribbon (harder, higher melting).
Fill in the blank: Then introduce the orbital argument: second period elements lack accessible d‑orbitals, limiting covalency to ______ and favouring pπ–pπ overlap.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can explain why lithium and beryllium show diagonal relationships with magnesium and aluminium respectively, predict the maximum covalency of second period elements versus heavier congeners, and justify the enhanced tendency of second period p‑block elements to form pπ–pπ multiple bonds using orbital size and energy arguments.
